title: Cryptography
body:
Cryptography spends a term using the algebra that [[ABSTRACT ALGEBRA]] spends a term building.
[[RSA]] is [[Modular Arithmetic]] with [[Lagrange's Theorem]] and the extended
[[Euclidean Algorithm]]. [[AES]] is arithmetic in $GF(2^8)$. [[Diffie-Hellman]] is
exponentiation in a [[Cyclic Group]], and [[Elliptic Curve Cryptography]] is the same protocol
with the group replaced. Very little new mathematics is introduced, and the work is seeing
where the existing mathematics lands.

The order is historical, from ciphers a pencil and a letter count defeat to the ones the
internet currently runs on. Every cipher along the way fell to a statistical or algebraic
structure its designers treated as unimportant, which is the pattern worth carrying out of the
course.

Two principles sit underneath everything. Kerckhoffs's principle states that the algorithm is
public and only the key is secret, so a scheme depending on nobody knowing how it works
provides nothing, since the algorithm leaks eventually and the key can be changed. The second
is to name the adversary: a claim that something is secure means nothing without a stated
attack model, and the discipline is to assume the strongest one available.

## Topics

### Classical ciphers and why they fail

[[Classical Ciphers]] covers the shift, affine, general substitution and Vigenère ciphers, all
of which are arithmetic in $\mathbb{Z}_{26}$ with letters numbered from 0.

```
shift by 3:   HELLO  ->  KHOOR          c = m + 3 mod 26
affine:       c = am + b mod 26          decryption needs a⁻¹, so gcd(a,26) = 1
```

That condition on $a$ is the invertibility theorem from [[Modular Arithmetic]] appearing in
week one: only the 12 values coprime to 26 are usable keys, because the others map two letters
to one and destroy the message. [[Transposition Cipher]] permutes positions and leaves the
characters alone, which puts both senses of [[Permutation]] in play at once, the count from
[[DISCRETE MATH]] and the structure from [[Permutation Group]].

[[Cryptanalysis]] holds the real content of the block. A general substitution cipher has $26!$
keys, about $4 \times 10^{26}$, and falls to a letter count in minutes, which establishes the
central lesson: the size of a key space says nothing on its own. What breaks it is that the
cipher preserves structure. English letter frequencies survive substitution unchanged, so the
most common ciphertext letter is probably `e`.

```
monoalphabetic   frequencies are preserved exactly, just relabelled
polyalphabetic   frequencies are flattened, because one letter maps several ways
transposition    frequencies are identical to plain English, since only order changed
```

Those three signatures identify which kind of cipher is in hand before any key is guessed. The
index of coincidence measures the flatness numerically, at $\approx 0.067$ for English and
$\approx 0.038$ for uniform text, so splitting a Vigenère ciphertext into the correct number of
columns makes each column's index jump back to the English value, which recovers the key
length. Kasiski examination reaches the same answer through repeated substrings. The block
also establishes the attack-model ladder, climbing from ciphertext-only through
known-plaintext and chosen-plaintext to chosen-ciphertext.

### Symmetric key cryptography

[[Symmetric Key Cryptography]] uses one shared key for both directions and is fast enough to
encrypt bulk data. The hub note covers the key distribution problem, which is that two parties
need a shared secret before they can communicate securely and establishing one over an insecure
channel is exactly the problem being solved.

Shannon named the two properties a good cipher needs. Confusion makes the relationship between
key and ciphertext complicated, and comes from substitution. Diffusion spreads the influence of
one plaintext bit across many ciphertext bits, and comes from permutation. A cipher that is
purely linear at any depth collapses to a single linear map and falls to linear algebra, which
is why every real design alternates non-linear and linear layers.

A block cipher is a keyed permutation of the block space and has to be a bijection, since
decryption is the inverse.

**[[Stream Cipher]]** encrypts by XOR against a generated keystream, so encryption and
decryption are the same operation:

```
0x41 ⊕ 0x1F = 0x5E          encrypt
0x5E ⊕ 0x1F = 0x41          decrypt, the same instruction
```

That is characteristic 2 arithmetic where $x + x = 0$, from [[ABSTRACT ALGEBRA]]. Reusing a
keystream is fatal for an algebraic reason: $c_1 \oplus c_2 = m_1 \oplus m_2$, the key cancels
entirely, and two plaintexts XORed together are readable by frequency analysis. The one-time
pad achieves perfect secrecy with a key as long as the message, which is why it is unusable at
scale. An LFSR is the classic keystream generator, a [[Shift Register]] with XOR feedback whose
period reaches $2^n - 1$ with a primitive tap polynomial, and $2n$ known keystream bits solve
for the whole thing, because it is linear.

**[[Feistel Network]]** makes any round function usable in an invertible cipher:

```
L(i+1) = R(i)
R(i+1) = L(i) ⊕ F(R(i), k(i))
```

$F$ is never inverted, so it need not be invertible, and decryption is the same circuit with
the subkeys reversed. DES is the standard example, and it died of a 56-bit key, with its
structure left unbroken. Double DES gains almost nothing, since meet-in-the-middle breaks it at
$2^{57}$ operations by trading memory for time.

**[[AES]]** is a substitution-permutation network on 128-bit blocks, running 10, 12 or 14
rounds for 128, 192 and 256-bit keys. Its state is a matrix of bytes, and a [[Byte]] here is an
element of $GF(2^8)$, where addition is XOR and multiplication is reduced modulo
$x^8+x^4+x^3+x+1$. Every non-zero byte has an inverse in that field, which $\mathbb{Z}_{256}$
cannot provide, and the S-box is exactly that inversion followed by an affine map. MixColumn is
a matrix product over the same field, so [[LINEAR ALGEBRA]] and [[Finite Field]] are both doing
load-bearing work inside a cipher shipping on every laptop.

**[[Modes of Operation]]** covers encrypting more than one block, and most deployment bugs live
here. ECB encrypts each block independently, so identical plaintext blocks produce identical
ciphertext blocks, which is monoalphabetic substitution one level up and leaves the outline of
an image visible after encryption. CBC chains each block into the next and needs an
unpredictable IV. CTR encrypts a counter to produce a keystream, which parallelises and needs
no padding, and repeating a nonce reproduces the keystream-reuse failure above. None of these
modes detects tampering, so integrity needs a MAC and the ordering is encrypt-then-MAC.

### Public key cryptography

[[Public Key Cryptography]] solves the key distribution problem with a trapdoor one-way
function: easy to compute, hard to invert, and easy to invert given a secret. The security
rests on an average-case hardness assumption, which no theorem establishes. Public-key
operations run roughly a thousand times slower per byte than symmetric ones, so every real
system is hybrid, using public key cryptography to agree a symmetric key and the symmetric
cipher for the data.

**[[RSA]]** with small primes, so every step is checkable:

```
p = 11, q = 13         n = pq = 143,  φ(n) = (p-1)(q-1) = 120
public exponent  e = 7          gcd(7, 120) = 1
private exponent d = 7⁻¹ mod 120 = 103        since 7 × 103 = 721 = 6(120) + 1

encrypt m = 9:   c = 9^7  mod 143 = 48
decrypt c = 48:  m = 48^103 mod 143 = 9
```

The decryption works because $ed \equiv 1 \pmod{\phi(n)}$, so $m^{ed} = m$ by Euler's theorem,
which is [[Lagrange's Theorem]] applied to the group of units mod $n$. The value $\phi(n)$ is
the trapdoor, and computing it requires the factorisation, so anyone who can factor $n$ can
read the traffic. The private exponent comes from the extended [[Euclidean Algorithm]], so
modular inversion and RSA key generation are the same computation. Modular exponentiation by
square-and-reduce costs $O(\log e)$ multiplications with intermediates bounded by $n^2$, and
without it none of this is computable at real key sizes. Textbook RSA is deterministic and
therefore broken, since an attacker can encrypt guesses and compare, so OAEP padding for
encryption and PSS for signatures are required parts of the scheme.

**[[Discrete Logarithm Problem]]** is the other hardness assumption: given $g^x = h$ in a
cyclic group, recover $x$. Generic attacks cost $O(\sqrt{n})$, and Pohlig-Hellman reduces the
problem to the largest prime factor of the group order, which is the argument for a safe prime
and a prime-order subgroup. Neither factoring nor discrete log is known to be [[NP-Complete]],
and NP-hardness describes the worst case while cryptography needs the average case to be hard.

**[[Diffie-Hellman]]** agrees a shared secret over an open channel:

```
public: p = 23, g = 5
Alice picks a = 6, sends  A = 5^6  mod 23 = 8
Bob   picks b = 15, sends B = 5^15 mod 23 = 19

Alice computes B^a = 19^6  mod 23 = 2
Bob   computes A^b = 8^15  mod 23 = 2        the same secret
```

Both arrive at $g^{ab}$ by different routes, and an eavesdropper holding $p$, $g$, 8 and 19 has
to solve the discrete logarithm to get there. It provides no authentication and falls to a man
in the middle who runs the exchange twice, and signing the exchange is the only repair, which
is the standing lesson about what mathematics leaves unsolved. The ephemeral variant provides
forward secrecy, so stealing a long-term key later fails to decrypt recorded sessions.
[[ElGamal]] turns the exchange into an encryption scheme, randomised by construction and
fatally sensitive to nonce reuse.

### Hashing and integrity

A [[Cryptographic Hash Function]] maps any input to a fixed-length digest and targets three
properties: pre-image resistance, second pre-image resistance and collision resistance, with
generic attack costs of $2^n$, $2^n$ and $2^{n/2}$.

Collision resistance is the cheapest to attack because the attacker chooses both messages,
which is the birthday bound: the number of pairs grows quadratically with the number of
messages, so $2^{n/2}$ attempts suffice. SHA-256 therefore provides 128 bits of collision
resistance, and the digest length is chosen at twice the intended security level for that
reason alone.

This kind of hash shares a name with [[Hashing]] in [[INFORMATION STRUCTURES]] and inverts its
design brief. A collision there is an expected event handled by chaining, and here it is a
break. Speed there is the goal, and here slowness is a feature that raises the cost of guessing
passwords.

Merkle-Damgård constructions leak through length extension, because the digest is the internal
state at the end of the message, so an attacker who knows $H(m)$ can compute $H(m \| x)$
without knowing $m$. That is why $H(k \| m)$ fails as a MAC and why [[HMAC]] nests two hash
calls. The sponge construction behind SHA-3 is immune by design. MD5 and SHA-1 are broken, and
SHA-2 and SHA-3 remain sound.

### Signatures

[[Digital Signature]] reverses the key roles, signing with the private key and verifying with
the public one, which is what supplies non-repudiation. A MAC proves only that the message came
from someone holding the shared key, so either party could have produced it and neither can
prove the other did.

A signature is computed over $H(m)$ for speed, which means a hash collision is a forgery: two
messages with the same digest have the same valid signature, and that is what retired SHA-1
from signing. The security target is existential unforgeability under adaptive chosen-message
attack, where the attacker gets a signing oracle and forging a signature on meaningless data
still counts as a break.

DSA requires a nonce $k$ that is fresh and secret. Reusing one across two signatures produces
two linear equations in two unknowns, and the private key falls out, which is how the PS3
signing key was recovered. Ed25519 derives its nonce deterministically from the message and the
key, removing the failure mode entirely.

### Elliptic curves and what comes next

[[Elliptic Curve Cryptography]] keeps every protocol and changes the group. The points on a
curve over a finite field form an abelian group under a geometric addition rule, and scalar
multiplication $kP$ replaces $g^k$. Index calculus is sub-exponential in $\mathbb{Z}_p^*$ and
has no analogue on elliptic curves, so the only known attacks are the generic $O(\sqrt{n})$
ones. That single missing algorithm is why a 256-bit elliptic curve key matches a 3072-bit RSA
key.

[[Post-Quantum Cryptography]] is the deadline. Shor's algorithm factors and solves discrete
logarithms in polynomial time on a quantum computer, breaking RSA, Diffie-Hellman and ECC
together, and its core is the quantum
[[Discrete Fourier Transform|Fourier transform]] used for period finding. Grover's algorithm
halves the effective key length of symmetric ciphers, so AES-256 survives at 128 bits and the
symmetric world needs only longer keys. The replacements are lattice-based schemes, hash-based
signatures and code-based schemes, the last of which reads [[Error Correcting Code]] as a
hardness assumption. Harvest now and decrypt later makes migration urgent for anything that
must stay secret for decades, since traffic recorded today can be stored until the hardware
exists. NIST standardised ML-KEM and ML-DSA in 2024, both lattice based, and deployments run
them alongside a classical scheme.

## Related courses

- [[ABSTRACT ALGEBRA]] is the stated prerequisite and supplies nearly everything.
  [[Modular Arithmetic]] gives $\mathbb{Z}_n$ and modular exponentiation, the extended
  [[Euclidean Algorithm]] is modular inversion and therefore RSA key generation,
  [[Lagrange's Theorem]] gives Fermat and Euler and therefore RSA correctness,
  [[Finite Field]] gives the $GF(2^8)$ the [[AES]] S-box inverts in, [[Cyclic Group]] is the
  object [[Diffie-Hellman]] and [[ElGamal]] run in, and [[Group]] with [[Irreducibility]]
  makes the curve group and the field construction legal.
- [[INFORMATION STRUCTURES]] owns the other meaning of hash in [[Hashing]] and
  [[Hash Function]]. The birthday argument is shared, forcing collision resolution on a hash
  table and a doubled digest length on a cryptographic hash. Baby-step giant-step, the
  standard [[Discrete Logarithm Problem]] attack, is a hash-table meet-in-the-middle.
- [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTABILITY]] supplies the complexity vocabulary, and this
  course adds the distinction between worst-case and average-case hardness that
  [[NP-Complete]] leaves open.
- [[COMPUTING MACHINERY 2]] is where the [[Stream Cipher]] block lands in
  hardware, since an LFSR is a [[Shift Register]] of [[Flip-Flop|flip-flops]] with XOR
  feedback and [[Boolean Algebra]] is $GF(2)$ from the circuit side.
- [[COMPUTING MACHINERY]] holds [[Error Detection]], and
  [[Integer Representation]] is arithmetic in $\mathbb{Z}_{2^n}$, the same modular reduction
  this course performs deliberately.
- [[STATISTICS]] is what [[Cryptanalysis]] consists of. Frequency analysis is a
  goodness-of-fit test, the index of coincidence is a collision [[Probability]], and the
  [[Chi-Square Test]] scores a candidate key. [[Random Numbers]] is the other half, since a
  keystream is a pseudo-random generator and a weak one has emptied real wallets through DSA
  nonce reuse.
- [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTER SCIENCE 2]] implements the number theory in
  [[Prime Number]], [[GCD and LCM]] and [[Division Algorithm]].
- [[FOURIER AND COMPLEX ANALYSIS]] meets this course inside Shor's algorithm,
  where the [[Discrete Fourier Transform]] performs the period finding and the
  [[Roots of Unity]] behind the [[Fast Fourier Transform]] are the cyclic structure a discrete
  logarithm hides in.
- [[LINEAR ALGEBRA]] does real work in two places, since MixColumn is a
  [[Matrix]]-vector product over $GF(2^8)$ and lattice-based cryptography is a
  [[Vector Space]] question with integer coefficients.
- [[THE NEW TURING OMNIBUS]] covers this material in one chapter as [[Cryptography]], and its
  [[Error Correcting Code]] is the same finite-field algebra aimed at noise, which McEliece
  turns back into a cryptosystem.
- [[WEB DEVELOPMENT FOR CS]] is where all of this is deployed. An [[HTTPS]]
  connection is an ephemeral [[Diffie-Hellman]] exchange authenticated by a chain of
  [[Digital Signature|signatures]] up to a [[Certificate Authority]], deriving an [[AES]] key
  that encrypts the [[HTTP]] traffic in an authenticated [[Modes of Operation|mode]]. The
  cipher supplies confidentiality, the [[HMAC|MAC]] supplies integrity, and the signature
  supplies authentication.
